orig_trigonometry_equations.description: One calculator result is a starting point. Use the graph, signs and interval to find every allowed angle.

sections.title: How do I find every angle from one trig value?
sections.label: One value, every angle
sections.intro:
First isolate the trigonometric ratio. Then ask which angles on the stated interval give that value. A calculator gives one principal angle; a graph or the unit circle shows the other possibilities.

  1. Check the angle unit and the interval.
  2. Isolate the sine, cosine or tangent.
  3. Find a principal or reference angle.
  4. Use signs and repetition to find every allowed angle.

blocks.html: A solution is an angle, not the trigonometric value. For example, \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\) is a condition on \(x\); it does not mean \(x=\frac{1}{2}\).
The line \(y=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) meets one full sine curve twice. Each intersection supplies an angle.
Do not stop at the calculator answer. Also do not add \(180^\circ\) automatically: sine and cosine do not repeat after half a turn.

blocks.title: Find the second angle
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Mark the horizontal level \(y=\frac{1}{2}\) on one full sine graph. How many crossings are there?
blocks.solution:
1. The reference angle is \(30^\circ\). Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants.

  2. The second angle is \(180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ\). Neither endpoint has sine equal to \(\frac{1}{2}\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{30,\ 150\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do cosine and tangent change the search?
sections.label: Cosine and tangent
sections.intro:
Use the coordinate meaning of each ratio. Cosine is positive on the right of the unit circle and negative on the left. Tangent is positive when sine and cosine have the same sign, and negative when their signs differ.

For an acute reference angle \(\alpha\), the negative cosine angles in one full turn are \(\pi-\alpha\) and \(\pi+\alpha\). Negative tangent angles in one full turn are \(\pi-\alpha\) and \(2\pi-\alpha\). Replace \(\pi\) by \(180^\circ\) when working in degrees.

blocks.html: Tangent repeats after \(\pi\) radians, or \(180^\circ\). Sine and cosine repeat after \(2\pi\) radians, or \(360^\circ\). Tangent is undefined wherever cosine is zero.
Cosine symmetry gives two angles at the same level. Tangent repeats its angle after \(\pi\), with gaps at its asymptotes.

blocks.title: Cosine in radians
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos x=-\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\). Give exact radian answers.
blocks.hint: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate on the unit circle. Find both points whose horizontal coordinate is \(-\frac{1}{2}\).
blocks.solution:
1. The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants.

  2. Use \(\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \frac{4 \pi}{3}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

blocks.title: A negative tangent angle
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\tan x=-1\) for \(-180^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Start at \(-45^\circ\), then move by one tangent period in each direction.
blocks.solution:
1. One angle is \(-45^\circ\). Tangent repeats after \(180^\circ\), giving \(135^\circ\).

  2. The next angles in either direction are outside the interval. The endpoints have tangent equal to zero.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{-45,\ 135\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I handle endpoints and more than one turn?
sections.label: Intervals and endpoints
sections.intro:
A graph does not stop after one turn. Extend the familiar pattern to the actual interval, including negative angles. Start from known solutions and move by complete periods until you have passed both ends.

Then read the inequalities carefully. A closed endpoint is a possible solution; an open endpoint is excluded even if it satisfies the equation. Keep two distinct endpoint values when both are allowed.

blocks.html: For \(\sin x=0\) on \(-\pi\le x\le2\pi\), all four marked angles are included.
Do not remove \(2\pi\) merely because it points in the same direction as zero. You are solving for values of the angle, not for distinct positions on a circle.

blocks.title: An excluded endpoint
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos x=1\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\). Give exact radian answers.
blocks.hint: Read the symbol at the right-hand endpoint before listing the full-turn angles.
blocks.solution:
1. Cosine equals one at the beginning and end of a complete turn: \(0\) and \(2\pi\).

  2. The upper inequality is strict, so \(2\pi\) is excluded.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

blocks.title: Both closed endpoints
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\tan x=0\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\). Give exact radian answers.
blocks.hint: The tangent period is \(\pi\), and both endpoint inequalities allow equality.
blocks.solution:
1. Tangent is zero at \(-\pi\), \(0\) and \(\pi\) in this interval.

  2. Both endpoints are included. They are different values of the unknown, even though a full-turn rotation returns to the same direction.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \pi,\ 0,\ \pi\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I solve an equation with a multiplied angle?
sections.label: Multiplied arguments
sections.intro:
If the argument is \(2x\), the sine or cosine completes two cycles while \(x\) completes one. Solving only over a single ordinary cycle can miss answers.

Introduce a temporary angle, transform the interval, solve for that angle, and then undo the substitution. Keep the interval beside every stage.

blocks.html: For \(u=2x\), the interval \(0\le x\le2\pi\) becomes \(0\le u\le4\pi\). After solving, divide every value of \(u\) by two.

blocks.title: A doubled argument
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos(2x)=-\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\). Give exact radian answers.
blocks.hint: Transform the interval before using the usual two cosine angles. The transformed interval contains two complete cycles.
blocks.solution:
1. Let \(u=2x\). The search interval becomes \(0\le u\le4\pi\).

  2. In this interval, \(u=\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3},\frac{8\pi}{3},\frac{10\pi}{3}\).

  3. Divide every angle by two to return to \(x\).

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \frac{4 \pi}{3},\ \frac{5 \pi}{3}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I handle a shift or a negative multiplier?
sections.label: Shifts and reversal
sections.intro:
Transform the entire argument, including the shift. For \(u=bx+c\), evaluate the argument at both original endpoints. If \(b\) is negative, the order reverses: put the smaller transformed endpoint first and preserve whether each endpoint is open or closed.

After finding every allowed value of \(u\), solve \(x=\frac{u-c}{b}\) for each and check the original interval.

blocks.html:
For \(u=2x-\frac\pi3\), map the endpoints of \(0\le x\le2\pi\) to \(-\frac\pi3\le u\le\frac{11\pi}{3}\). Solve \(\cos u=\frac12\) on that interval and convert each solution back to \(x\).

For \(u=2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\), transform the interval as well as each solution. Both original endpoints can survive.

blocks.title: A shifted doubled angle
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin(2x+30^\circ)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\).
blocks.hint: The transformed interval includes its two endpoints. Test both of them.
blocks.solution:
1. Let \(u=2x+30^\circ\), so \(30^\circ\le u\le390^\circ\).

  2. The allowed sine angles are \(u=30^\circ,150^\circ,390^\circ\).

  3. Use \(x=\frac{u-30^\circ}{2}\) for each.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0,\ 60,\ 180\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

blocks.html: Subtracting the shift from the final answer is not enough when the argument also has a multiplier. Undo both operations in the correct order.

blocks.title: A reversed interval
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\). Give exact radian answers.
blocks.hint: Evaluate the new argument at both endpoints, then put the smaller bound first.
blocks.solution:
1. Put \(u=\frac{\pi}{2}-x\). As \(x\) increases, \(u\) decreases. The ordered interval is \(-\frac{3\pi}{2}\le u\le\frac{\pi}{2}\).

  2. The valid cosine angles are \(u=-\frac{\pi}{3}\) and \(u=\frac{\pi}{3}\).

  3. Use \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}-u\), then sort the resulting angles.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I round and check a complete answer?
sections.label: Accuracy and checking
sections.intro:
For unfamiliar values, use the inverse function in the correct mode. Keep its full calculator value while constructing the other angles. Round only the final values of the original unknown.

Before using an inverse sine or cosine, check that the isolated value lies between \(-1\) and \(1\). For example, \(3\sin x=4\) has no real solution because \(\sin x=\frac{4}{3}\) is impossible.

blocks.html: Show the isolated ratio, the transformed interval when needed, and the angle-finding step. A list from a calculator does not show why the set is complete.
Finish with four checks: every value satisfies the original equation; every value lies in the original interval; no tangent input is undefined; the list has the required units and accuracy.

blocks.title: Round only the final angles
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin x=0.4\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\). Give each answer in radians to three decimal places.
blocks.hint: Use the unrounded calculator value for the second angle, not the rounded first answer.
blocks.solution:
1. In radian mode, keep \(\alpha=\sin^{-1}(0.4)\) unrounded.

  2. Sine is positive in the first two quadrants, so the angles are \(\alpha\) and \(\pi-\alpha\).

  3. Round both final angles to three decimal places.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0.412,\ 2.730\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

examples.title: A positive exact sine value
examples.question: Solve \(\sin x=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\).
solution:
The exact reference angle is \(60^\circ\).

Recall the special triangle values.

Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so \(x=60^\circ\) or \(x=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ\).

Both points have the required vertical coordinate.

Both values lie in the interval; the endpoints have sine zero. The complete answer is \(\{60^\circ,120^\circ\}\).

A full cycle contains no further crossings at this level.

examples.title: A negative sine value
examples.question: Solve \(2\sin x+1=0\) for \(0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\).
solution: Rearrange to \(\sin x=-\frac{1}{2}\). The reference angle is \(30^\circ\).
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants. Use \(180^\circ+30^\circ=210^\circ\) and \(360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ\).
Thus \(x=210^\circ\) or \(x=330^\circ\). The calculator value \(-30^\circ\) is outside this interval, but it identifies the same sine level.

examples.title: Negative cosine in radians
examples.question: Solve \(\cos x=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants.
Therefore \(x=\pi-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{3\pi}{4}\) or \(x=\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{5\pi}{4}\).
Both values lie in the interval and both have the required negative cosine.

examples.title: Tangent repeats sooner
examples.question: Solve \(\tan x=-\sqrt3\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
solution: The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants.
The first solution is \(x=\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}\). Add the tangent period \(\pi\) to get \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\).
Thus the complete set is \(\left\{\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{3}\right\}\). Neither solution is an undefined tangent input.

examples.title: A closed interval longer than one turn
examples.question: Solve \(\sin x=0\) for \(-\pi\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: The sine graph crosses its axis at \(-\pi\), \(0\), \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\) in the required interval.
The endpoint inequalities allow equality, so keep \(-\pi\) and \(2\pi\).
The complete answer is \(\{-\pi,0,\pi,2\pi\}\). These are four different values of the unknown.

examples.title: Two cycles inside the interval
examples.question: Solve \(\sin(2x)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\).
solution: Put \(u=2x\). Then \(0^\circ\le u\le720^\circ\).
In the first cycle, \(u=30^\circ,150^\circ\). The second cycle gives \(u=390^\circ,510^\circ\).
Divide each value by two: \(x=15^\circ,75^\circ,195^\circ,255^\circ\).
Every answer lies in the original interval. Substituting each doubled angle gives sine equal to \(\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: A shifted cosine with five answers
examples.question: Solve \(\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: Let \(u=2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\). The interval becomes \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\le u\le\frac{11\pi}{3}\).
The cosine angles in this interval are \(u=-\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{3},\frac{7\pi}{3},\frac{11\pi}{3}\).
Use \(x=\frac{u+\frac{\pi}{3}}{2}\). This gives \(x=0,\frac{\pi}{3},\pi,\frac{4\pi}{3},2\pi\).
Both original endpoints satisfy the equation and are included. Five answers are correct here.

examples.title: The argument runs backwards
examples.question: Solve \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-2x\right)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\).
solution: Set \(u=\frac{\pi}{6}-2x\). At the endpoints, \(u=\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(u=-\frac{11\pi}{6}\), so \(-\frac{11\pi}{6}\le u\le\frac{\pi}{6}\).
The allowed sine angles are \(u=-\frac{11\pi}{6},-\frac{7\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6}\).
Use \(x=\frac{\frac{\pi}{6}-u}{2}\). The corresponding values are \(\pi,\frac{2\pi}{3},0\).
List the complete set in increasing order: \(\left\{0,\frac{2\pi}{3},\pi\right\}\).

examples.title: An approximate answer on a symmetric interval
examples.question: Solve \(\cos x=0.3\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\), giving radians to three decimal places.
solution: Use radian mode and store \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}(0.3)\approx1.266103673\).
Cosine is even, so both \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\) have the required value. They are the only crossings in the interval.
To three decimal places, \(x=-1.266\) or \(x=1.266\).

glossary.definition: The single angle returned by an inverse trigonometric function in its chosen range.
The acute angle between the terminal radius and the horizontal axis.
The allowed values of the unknown; \(\le\) includes an endpoint and \(<\) excludes it.
The horizontal distance after which a graph repeats: \(2\pi\) for sine and cosine, \(\pi\) for tangent.
A new angle such as \(u=2x+\frac{\pi}{3}\), whose interval must also be calculated.
Every allowed value, with no missing angles, excluded values or repeated entries.

extraPractice.title: Isolate an exact sine
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(2\sin x=\sqrt2\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\).
extraPractice.hint: First isolate \(\sin x\), then use the sign to choose quadrants.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Divide by two: \(\sin x=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\), with reference angle \(45^\circ\).

  2. Sine is positive in the first two quadrants, so use \(45^\circ\) and \(180^\circ-45^\circ\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{45,\ 135\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Cosine on a negative-to-positive interval
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\cos x=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Sketch the cosine curve on the actual interval, including its negative half.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The positive principal angle is \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\).

  2. Cosine is even, so the negative angle \(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\) also works. The interval contains no other crossings.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \frac{5 \pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Three tangent solutions
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\tan x=\sqrt3\) for \(-180^\circ<x\le360^\circ\).
extraPractice.hint: Tangent repeats after half a turn. Search to the left as well as to the right.
extraPractice.solution:
1. One angle is \(60^\circ\). Move by tangent periods of \(180^\circ\).

  2. The angles \(-120^\circ,60^\circ,240^\circ\) lie in the interval; the adjacent possibilities \(-300^\circ\) and \(420^\circ\) do not.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{-120,\ 60,\ 240\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: A sine minimum over two turns
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin x=-1\) for \(-\frac{3\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{5\pi}{2}\).
extraPractice.hint: A maximum and a minimum do not give two separate crossings at the same point.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The sine minimum occurs at \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\), then repeats after \(2\pi\), giving \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\).

  2. The endpoints have sine equal to one, so neither is a solution.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3 \pi}{2}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: One open and one closed endpoint
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\cos x=0\) for \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\le x<\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
extraPractice.hint: List the cosine zeros first, then apply the endpoint symbols.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The candidate zeros are \(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\).

  2. Include the left endpoint and exclude the strict right endpoint.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{\pi}{2}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Three times the angle
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin(3x)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: The transformed interval extends beyond one full turn.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Let \(u=3x\), so \(0\le u\le3\pi\).

  2. The allowed angles are \(u=\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{13\pi}{6},\frac{17\pi}{6}\).

  3. Divide each by three.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{18},\ \frac{5 \pi}{18},\ \frac{13 \pi}{18},\ \frac{17 \pi}{18}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: A shifted tangent
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\tan\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Transform the interval, then use the tangent period \(\pi\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. Let \(u=x-\frac{\pi}{4}\). Then \(-\frac{\pi}{4}\le u<\frac{7\pi}{4}\).

  2. Tangent equals one at \(u=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\) in that interval.

  3. Add \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) to each value to recover \(x\).

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3 \pi}{2}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: A negative multiplier in degrees
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\cos(60^\circ-2x)=\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\).
extraPractice.hint: Evaluate the argument at both endpoints before ordering the transformed interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. For \(u=60^\circ-2x\), the ordered interval is \(-300^\circ\le u\le60^\circ\).

  2. The valid values are \(u=-300^\circ,-60^\circ,60^\circ\).

  3. Use \(x=\frac{60^\circ-u}{2}\), giving \(180^\circ,60^\circ,0^\circ\), then sort.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0,\ 60,\ 180\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Approximate cosine angles
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(4\cos x-1=0\) for \(-180^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\). Give answers to one decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Cosine is symmetric about the vertical axis.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Isolate \(\cos x=\frac{1}{4}\). In degree mode, \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\).

  2. The two angles are \(-\alpha\) and \(\alpha\). Round only these final values.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{-75.5,\ 75.5\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Check whether a solution can exist
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(3\sin x-4=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Check the range of sine before pressing an inverse-function key.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Rearranging gives \(\sin x=\frac{4}{3}\).

  2. A sine value cannot exceed one, so no real angle satisfies the equation.

  3. The solution set is \(\varnothing\): there are no solutions in the stated interval.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

starters.title: A shifted sine over a full original turn
starters.question: Solve \(2\sin\left(2x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\sqrt3\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\). Give exact radian answers.
starters.hint: Keep the right endpoint open after transforming the interval.
starters.solution:
1. Put \(u=2x+\frac{\pi}{6}\). Then \(\frac{\pi}{6}\le u<\frac{25\pi}{6}\), and \(\sin u=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).

  2. The allowed values are \(u=\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{7\pi}{3},\frac{8\pi}{3}\).

  3. Apply \(x=\frac{u-\frac{\pi}{6}}{2}\) to every value.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{12},\ \frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{13 \pi}{12},\ \frac{5 \pi}{4}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: isolate \(\sin u=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), with \(u=2x+\frac{\pi}{6}\).
  • 1 mark: transform the interval to \(\frac{\pi}{6}\le u<\frac{25\pi}{6}\), preserving the open endpoint.
  • 1 mark: identify all four allowed values of \(u\).
  • 1 mark: apply \(x=\frac{u-\frac{\pi}{6}}{2}\) to every candidate.
  • 1 mark: give the complete exact set \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{12},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{13\pi}{12},\frac{5\pi}{4}\right\}\).

starters.title: A tangent equation including both endpoints
starters.question: Solve \(\tan(3x-45^\circ)=-1\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\).
starters.hint: Move in steps of \(180^\circ\) in the transformed angle.
starters.solution:
1. Let \(u=3x-45^\circ\). The interval becomes \(-45^\circ\le u\le495^\circ\).

  2. Starting at \(-45^\circ\), tangent periods give \(u=-45^\circ,135^\circ,315^\circ,495^\circ\).

  3. Use \(x=\frac{u+45^\circ}{3}\). Both original endpoints are valid and included.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0,\ 60,\ 120,\ 180\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use \(u=3x-45^\circ\) and obtain \(-45^\circ\le u\le495^\circ\).
  • 1 mark: recognise the tangent period \(180^\circ\) and a valid starting angle.
  • 1 mark: obtain \(u=-45^\circ,135^\circ,315^\circ,495^\circ\), including both endpoints.
  • 1 mark: use \(x=\frac{u+45^\circ}{3}\) for each value.
  • 1 mark: give \(x=0^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ,180^\circ\) with no additional values.

starters.title: A shifted interval running backwards
starters.question: Solve \(2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-2x\right)+1=0\) for \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\le x\le\frac{2\pi}{3}\).
starters.hint: Put the transformed endpoints in increasing order after applying the negative multiplier.
starters.solution:
1. Set \(u=\frac{\pi}{3}-2x\). The endpoint values are \(\pi\) and \(-\pi\), so \(-\pi\le u\le\pi\).

  2. Now \(\cos u=-\frac{1}{2}\), giving \(u=-\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

  3. Use \(x=\frac{\frac{\pi}{3}-u}{2}\), giving \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\).

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{\pi}{2}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: isolate \(\cos u=-\frac{1}{2}\), where \(u=\frac{\pi}{3}-2x\).
  • 1 mark: evaluate both transformed endpoints and order them as \(-\pi\le u\le\pi\).
  • 1 mark: find \(u=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\) and \(u=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).
  • 1 mark: return to the original variable using \(x=\frac{\frac{\pi}{3}-u}{2}\).
  • 1 mark: give the complete set \(\left\{-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{2}\right\}\).

starters.title: Approximation after undoing the argument
starters.question: Solve \(\sin(2x-0.4)=0.6\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\). Angles are in radians. Give answers to three decimal places.
starters.hint: Round after adding the shift and dividing by the multiplier.
starters.solution:
1. Let \(u=2x-0.4\). Then \(-0.4\le u\le2\pi-0.4\).

  2. With \(\alpha=\sin^{-1}(0.6)\), the allowed angles are \(u=\alpha\) and \(u=\pi-\alpha\).

  3. Use \(x=\frac{u+0.4}{2}\) with unrounded values, then round the final results.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0.522,\ 1.449\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: use \(u=2x-0.4\) and obtain \(-0.4\le u\le2\pi-0.4\).
  • 1 mark: calculate or retain \(\alpha=\sin^{-1}(0.6)\) in radian mode.
  • 1 mark: identify both allowed angles, \(u=\alpha\) and \(u=\pi-\alpha\).
  • 1 mark: use \(x=\frac{u+0.4}{2}\) with unrounded values.
  • 1 mark: give both final radian answers to three decimal places, with no extra solutions.

revision.body:
Isolate, then locate

First isolate the ratio. Sine and cosine values must lie in \([-1,1]\). A calculator returns one principal angle; use signs, symmetry and the graph for the rest.

Sine is positive above the horizontal axis; cosine is positive to the right; tangent is positive where both have the same sign.

Repeat across the actual interval

Sine and cosine repeat after \(2\pi\) or \(360^\circ\); tangent after \(\pi\) or \(180^\circ\). Search negative angles and extra cycles when required. Tangent is undefined when cosine is zero.

Include endpoints marked \(\le\); exclude endpoints marked \(<\). Distinct endpoint angles can both belong to the answer.

Transform the whole argument

For \(u=bx+c\), evaluate \(u\) at both original endpoints. Put the smaller endpoint first; a negative multiplier reverses the order. Preserve which endpoints are open or closed.

Solve throughout the transformed interval, then use

\[x=\frac{u-c}{b}.\]

Apply this to every value and recheck the original interval.

Exact values and accuracy

Keep exact multiples of \(\pi\) when asked. For unfamiliar values, use the stated calculator mode and store the unrounded inverse value. Round only the final original angles.

A sketch checks completeness; substitution checks validity. Show the interval transformation and the angle-finding step in written work.
revision.checks:
• Have I found every crossing, including negative angles and further cycles?
  • Did I preserve the endpoint inequalities?
  • Did I undo the whole argument for every solution?
  • Are tangent values defined and sine or cosine values within \([-1,1]\)?
  • Are the units, exact form and final rounding correct?
revision.examTip: State the interval before solving. Include all allowed angles and follow the requested accuracy and angle units.

orig_trigonometry_quadratic_equations.description: Solve the algebra first, decide which trig values are possible, then find every allowed angle for each branch.

sections.title: How does substitution turn the equation into a quadratic?
sections.label: Algebra before angles
sections.intro:
When the same trigonometric expression appears squared and unsquared, temporarily treat it as one number. For example, with \(t=\sin x\), the expression \(2\sin^2x-3\sin x+1\) becomes \(2t^2-3t+1\).

After solving for the temporary variable, return to the trigonometric ratio and find every angle in the stated interval. Keep these as two separate stages.

blocks.html: \(\sin^2x\) means \((\sin x)^2\). It does not mean \(\sin(x^2)\), and it does not mean \(\sin(2x)\).

blocks.title: Two cosine values
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\cos^2x+\cos x-1=0\) for \(0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Factor the quadratic in a temporary variable before finding angles.
blocks.solution:
1. Put \(t=\cos x\). Factor \(2t^2+t-1=(2t-1)(t+1)=0\).

  2. Thus \(\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\) or \(\cos x=-1\). These give \(60^\circ,300^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{60,\ 180,\ 300\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: Which quadratic roots can become angles?
sections.label: Valid branches
sections.intro:
The polynomial may produce values that no sine or cosine can take. Keep only values in \([-1,1]\) for those two ratios. Tangent has no such bounded range, but its angle must still avoid undefined inputs.

The number of algebraic roots is not the number of angle solutions. Each valid ratio value can occur at several angles, and a repeated algebraic root is processed only once.

blocks.html:
The shaded interval shows \(-1\le\cos x\le1\). Of the polynomial roots \(t=-2\) and \(t=\frac12\), only the latter is a possible cosine value.

The polynomial \(2t^2+3t-2\) has two real roots, but only \(t=\frac{1}{2}\) lies in the cosine range \([-1,1]\).

blocks.title: A valid endpoint branch
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cos^2x-4\cos x+3=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
blocks.hint: Reject an impossible ratio, then read both endpoint inequalities for the remaining branch.
blocks.solution:
1. Put \(t=\cos x\). Then \((t-1)(t-3)=0\), so \(t=1\) or \(t=3\).

  2. Reject \(t=3\), which is outside the cosine range. The branch \(\cos x=1\) gives both included endpoints \(0\) and \(2\pi\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0,\ 2 \pi\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

blocks.html:
The repeated polynomial root from \((2t-1)^2=0\) is \(t=\frac12\). When \(t=\sin x\), it corresponds to two distinct angles on one complete turn.

One repeated polynomial root, \(t=\frac{1}{2}\), still gives two sine angles in one full turn.

blocks.title: A repeated algebraic root
blocks.prompt: Solve \(4\sin^2x+4\sin x+1=0\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
blocks.hint: A repeated root of the polynomial does not mean there is only one angle.
blocks.solution:
1. The quadratic is \((2\sin x+1)^2=0\), so the only ratio value is \(\sin x=-\frac{1}{2}\).

  2. That one ratio value occurs at two angles in this interval: \(\frac{7\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{7 \pi}{6},\ \frac{11 \pi}{6}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I combine sine and cosine safely?
sections.label: Use one ratio
sections.intro:
A squared ratio can often be replaced by the basic identity. If the unsquared term is cosine, use \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\). If it is sine, use \(\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x\). This leaves a quadratic in just one ratio.

Do not replace \(\sin x\) by \(1-\cos x\). The identity concerns the squares.

blocks.title: Use an identity before factorising
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\cos^2x-3\sin x=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
blocks.hint: The unsquared term is sine, so replace the squared cosine using the identity.
blocks.solution:
1. Use \(\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x\), giving \(2\sin^2x+3\sin x-2=0\).

  2. Factor \((2\sin x-1)(\sin x+2)=0\). The value \(\sin x=-2\) is impossible.

  3. The remaining branch \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\) gives the two first-half-turn angles.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

blocks.html: The restriction \(-1\le t\le1\) is for sine and cosine values. A tangent value such as \(t=2\) is valid.

blocks.title: Both tangent branches
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\tan^2x-1=0\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
blocks.hint: Tangent can take any real value; use both factors and its period \(\pi\).
blocks.solution:
1. Factor \((\tan x-1)(\tan x+1)=0\), so \(\tan x=1\) or \(\tan x=-1\).

  2. Each tangent value occurs twice on this interval. None of the resulting angles is a tangent asymptote.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{3 \pi}{4},\ \frac{5 \pi}{4},\ \frac{7 \pi}{4}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I keep roots when a factor can be zero?
sections.label: Keep zero factors
sections.intro: When a trigonometric factor occurs on both sides, bring everything to one side and factor. The zero-product rule keeps every branch. Dividing by a factor assumes it is nonzero and can remove valid angles.

blocks.html: The equation \(2\sin x\cos x-\sin x=0\) has five roots on \([0,2\pi]\). The zero-sine branch supplies three of them.
Factor first. Solve each factor equation. Combine the angle sets and list every distinct angle once.

blocks.title: Do not divide away a factor
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\sin x\cos x=\sin x\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
blocks.hint: Use the zero-product rule instead of dividing by \(\sin x\).
blocks.solution:
1. Bring everything to one side and factor: \(\sin x(2\cos x-1)=0\).

  2. The branch \(\sin x=0\) gives \(0,\pi,2\pi\). The branch \(\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{3}\).

  3. Combine both branches. Dividing by sine at the start would lose three answers.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0,\ \frac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \frac{5 \pi}{3},\ 2 \pi\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do denominators and squaring change the final check?
sections.label: Restrictions and candidates
sections.intro: A fraction is zero when its numerator is zero and its denominator is nonzero. Record the original denominator restriction before multiplying or cancelling. A simplified expression does not restore an angle excluded by the original one.

blocks.title: Keep a denominator restriction
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\frac{\cos^2x-\cos x}{\cos x}=0\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\).
blocks.hint: Record where the denominator is zero before cancelling anything.
blocks.solution:
1. The original expression requires \(\cos x\ne0\).

  2. Factor the numerator as \(\cos x(\cos x-1)\). Under the restriction, the equation reduces to \(\cos x-1=0\).

  3. Only \(x=0\) satisfies \(\cos x=1\) in the interval. The angles \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) make the original denominator zero and are excluded.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

blocks.html: Squaring an equation can add candidates because it removes sign information. It is a useful algebraic step only if every candidate is checked in the original equation.

After squaring \(\sin x=2\cos x\), check the original signs. With \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}2\), keep \(\alpha\) and \(\pi+\alpha\) because the sine and cosine signs agree. The other two candidates have opposite signs.

Squaring \(\sin x=2\cos x\) finds four candidate points. Only the two where sine and cosine have the same sign satisfy the original equation.

blocks.title: Check candidates after squaring
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\sin x=\cos x\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
blocks.hint: Squaring hides the signs. Substitute the candidates into the original equation.
blocks.solution:
1. Squaring gives \(\sin^2x=\cos^2x\), hence \(\cos^2x=\frac{1}{2}\). This produces the four candidates \(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4},\frac{7\pi}{4}\).

  2. In the original equation, sine and cosine must have the same sign. Reject the second- and fourth-quadrant candidates.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{5 \pi}{4}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

sections.title: How do I combine a transformed argument and the quadratic formula?
sections.label: Combine the methods
sections.intro:
Use the same order even when the algebra does not factor neatly: transform the angle interval, solve the polynomial in a ratio value, reject impossible values, find all allowed angles, and undo the argument.

Two temporary variables can help: one for the angle and one for its trigonometric value. Name their roles clearly.

blocks.html: Keep the quadratic root exact until evaluating the inverse function. Show the rejected branch and its reason. Then show the interval search for every surviving branch.

blocks.title: Two ratio branches and a multiplied argument
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\sin^2(3x)-3\sin(3x)+1=0\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\).
blocks.hint: Search the whole transformed interval for each valid ratio value.
blocks.solution:
1. Put \(u=3x\), so \(0\le u\le3\pi\). Factor \((2\sin u-1)(\sin u-1)=0\).

  2. For \(\sin u=\frac{1}{2}\), use \(u=\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{13\pi}{6},\frac{17\pi}{6}\). For \(\sin u=1\), use \(u=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{5\pi}{2}\).

  3. Divide all six angles by three, combine the branches and sort.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{18},\ \frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{18},\ \frac{13 \pi}{18},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6},\ \frac{17 \pi}{18}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

examples.title: Two sine values, three angles
examples.question: Solve \(2\sin^2x-3\sin x+1=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: The algebra gives \(t=\frac{1}{2}\) or \(t=1\). Both lie in the sine range \([-1,1]\).
For \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\), the angles are \(\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6}\). For \(\sin x=1\), the angle is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
The complete set is \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{5\pi}{6}\right\}\).

examples.title: An impossible cosine value
examples.question: Solve \(2\cos^2x+3\cos x-2=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: The values are \(t=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(t=-2\). Reject \(-2\), because cosine cannot be less than \(-1\).
For \(\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\), the interval solutions are \(x=\frac{\pi}{3}\) and \(x=\frac{5\pi}{3}\).

examples.title: A repeated root is not one angle
examples.question: Solve \((2\sin x-1)^2=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: The squared factor is zero only when \(2\sin x-1=0\), so \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\).
The ratio value is repeated algebraically, but the sine graph reaches that value at \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\).
List each angle once: \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6}\right\}\).

examples.title: Convert the squared ratio
examples.question: Solve \(2\sin^2x+3\cos x=0\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\).
solution: Replace the squared sine: \(2(1-\cos^2x)+3\cos x=0\).
Rearrange and factor: \(2\cos^2x-3\cos x-2=(2\cos x+1)(\cos x-2)=0\).
The values are \(\cos x=-\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos x=2\). Reject the second.
Negative cosine with reference angle \(60^\circ\) gives \(x=120^\circ,240^\circ\).

examples.title: A quadratic in tangent
examples.question: Solve \(\tan^2x-3\tan x+2=0\) for \(0\le x<\pi\). Give exact answers, allowing inverse trigonometric notation.
solution: Factor \((\tan x-1)(\tan x-2)=0\). Both ratio values are possible for tangent.
The branch \(\tan x=1\) gives \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\). The branch \(\tan x=2\) gives \(x=\tan^{-1}(2)\).
Both angles lie in the first quadrant. Adding a tangent period would leave the interval. The complete set is \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{4},\tan^{-1}(2)\right\}\).

examples.title: A shared angle from two factors
examples.question: Solve \(\sin x\cos x=\cos x\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: Rearrange to \(\cos x(\sin x-1)=0\).
For \(\cos x=0\), the angles are \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\). For \(\sin x=1\), the angle is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Combine the branches and remove the repeated entry: \(x\in\left\{\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right\}\).
Direct substitution confirms both. Dividing by cosine at the start would assume away its zero branch.

examples.title: A factor that must not be zero
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{2\sin^2x-\sin x}{\sin x}=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
solution: The original denominator requires \(\sin x\ne0\), excluding \(0,\pi,2\pi\).
Factor the numerator: \(\frac{\sin x(2\sin x-1)}{\sin x}=0\). On the allowed domain, cancel to get \(2\sin x-1=0\).
Thus \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\), so \(x=\frac{\pi}{6}\) or \(x=\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Both satisfy the original restriction.

examples.title: Squaring creates two extra candidates
examples.question: Solve \(\sin x=2\cos x\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\). Give exact answers using inverse trigonometric notation.
solution: Squaring gives \(\sin^2x=4\cos^2x\). Use the identity to obtain \(\cos^2x=\frac{1}{5}\).
Let \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(2)\), an acute angle. The squared equation has candidates \(\alpha,\pi-\alpha,\pi+\alpha,2\pi-\alpha\).
The original equation requires sine and cosine to have the same sign. Keep the first and third quadrants; reject the other two.
Therefore \(x=\tan^{-1}(2)\) or \(x=\pi+\tan^{-1}(2)\). Alternatively, first show cosine cannot be zero, then divide safely to obtain \(\tan x=2\).

examples.title: A quadratic formula inside a doubled angle
examples.question: Solve \(2\cos^2(2x)+\cos(2x)-2=0\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\). Give radians to three decimal places.
solution: Let \(u=2x\), so \(0\le u\le2\pi\). Then let \(t=\cos u\).
Store \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{4}\right)\). The two transformed angles are \(u=\alpha\) and \(u=2\pi-\alpha\).
Return to \(x\): \(x=\frac{\alpha}{2}\) or \(x=\pi-\frac{\alpha}{2}\). To three decimal places, \(x=0.337\) or \(x=2.804\).

glossary.definition: Replace a repeated expression by a temporary variable, for example \(t=\sin x\).
One ratio equation obtained from the algebra, such as \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\).
A ratio value that belongs to the range of the trigonometric function and satisfies the original restrictions.
One polynomial value occurring twice in a factorisation; it may still correspond to several angles.
An angle at which the original expression is undefined, even if a simplified expression can be evaluated.
A possible answer produced by a method such as squaring; it must pass the original equation.

related.title: All solutions on a stated interval

extraPractice.title: A positive and a negative sine value
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(2\sin^2x+\sin x-1=0\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\).
extraPractice.hint: Find the sine values first, then solve each branch on the interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Factor \((2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)=0\).

  2. The branch \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(30^\circ,150^\circ\); the branch \(\sin x=-1\) gives \(270^\circ\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{30,\ 150,\ 270\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Cosine branches across zero
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(2\cos^2x-3\cos x+1=0\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Cosine is even. Search both halves of the stated interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Factor \((2\cos x-1)(\cos x-1)=0\).

  2. For \(\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\), use \(\pm\frac{\pi}{3}\). For \(\cos x=1\), use zero.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \frac{\pi}{3},\ 0,\ \frac{\pi}{3}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: No real ratio root
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin^2x+\sin x+1=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Check the quadratic discriminant before looking for angles.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Put \(t=\sin x\). The discriminant of \(t^2+t+1\) is \(1-4=-3\).

  2. The polynomial has no real root, so it cannot supply a real sine value.

  3. The solution set is \(\varnothing\): there are no solutions in the stated interval.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: One repeated cosine value
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(4\cos^2x-4\cos x+1=0\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Solve the repeated factor once; then find every corresponding angle.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The equation is \((2\cos x-1)^2=0\), giving \(\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\).

  2. The two angle solutions are in the first and fourth quadrants.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{5 \pi}{3}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Identity and approximate angles
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(3\sin^2x+\cos x-1=0\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\). Give non-integer angles to one decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Do not lose either endpoint of the \(\cos x=1\) branch.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Use \(\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x\), giving \(3\cos^2x-\cos x-2=0\).

  2. Factor \((3\cos x+2)(\cos x-1)=0\). Thus \(\cos x=-\frac{2}{3}\) or \(\cos x=1\).

  3. For the first branch, use \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)\) in degrees and \(360^\circ-\alpha\). The second branch gives both included endpoints.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0.0,\ 131.8,\ 228.2,\ 360.0\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: An unrestricted tangent value
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\tan^2x+2\tan x-3=0\) for \(-\frac{\pi}{2}<x<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Give exact answers, allowing inverse trigonometric notation.
extraPractice.hint: Tangent can equal \(-3\); its range is not restricted to \([-1,1]\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. Factor \((\tan x+3)(\tan x-1)=0\).

  2. On this principal tangent interval, the unique angles are \(-\tan^{-1}(3)\) and \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). Both are strictly between the asymptotes.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \tan^{-1}{\left(3 \right)},\ \frac{\pi}{4}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Two factors on a symmetric interval
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin x(2\cos x+1)=0\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Solve both factors, preserving the included endpoints.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Use \(\sin x=0\) or \(\cos x=-\frac{1}{2}\).

  2. The sine branch gives \(-\pi,0,\pi\); the cosine branch gives \(-\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{- \pi,\ - \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ 0,\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \pi\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: A cancelled branch is forbidden
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\frac{2\cos^2x+\cos x-1}{2\cos x-1}=0\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the denominator restriction before using the factorisation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The denominator requires \(\cos x\ne\frac{1}{2}\).

  2. Factor the numerator: \((2\cos x-1)(\cos x+1)\). On the allowed domain, the equation reduces to \(\cos x+1=0\).

  3. The surviving angle is \(x=\pi\). Angles from the cancelled factor were excluded in the original expression.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\pi\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Restore the lost sign information
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sin x=-\cos x\) for \(0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\).
extraPractice.hint: Check the signs in the original equation, not only the squared equation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Squaring gives \(\cos^2x=\frac{1}{2}\), with candidates \(45^\circ,135^\circ,225^\circ,315^\circ\).

  2. The original equation requires opposite signs for sine and cosine. Keep the second and fourth quadrants.

  3. Therefore \(x\in \left\{135,\ 315\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

extraPractice.title: Use the quadratic formula
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(2\sin^2x+2\sin x-1=0\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\). Give radians to three decimal places.
extraPractice.hint: Keep the exact surd while evaluating the inverse sine.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Put \(t=\sin x\). The quadratic formula gives \(t=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt3}{2}\).

  2. Reject \(\frac{-1-\sqrt3}{2}<-1\). For the other value, store \(\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt3}{2}\right)\).

  3. The two angles are \(\alpha\) and \(\pi-\alpha\). Round these final values.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0.375,\ 2.767\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

starters.title: A shifted quadratic in cosine
starters.question: Solve \(2\cos^2\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+3\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+1=0\) for \(0\le x\le\pi\).
starters.hint: Keep the two ratio branches separate until each interval search is complete.
starters.solution:
1. Let \(u=2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\), so \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\le u\le\frac{5\pi}{3}\).

  2. Factor \((2\cos u+1)(\cos u+1)=0\), giving \(\cos u=-\frac{1}{2}\) or \(\cos u=-1\).

  3. The transformed angles are \(u=\frac{2\pi}{3},\pi,\frac{4\pi}{3}\). Apply \(x=\frac{u+\frac{\pi}{3}}{2}\) to each.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: let \(u=2x-\frac{\pi}{3}\) and obtain \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\le u\le\frac{5\pi}{3}\).
  • 1 mark: factor the quadratic as \((2\cos u+1)(\cos u+1)=0\).
  • 1 mark: obtain both valid branches, \(\cos u=-\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos u=-1\).
  • 1 mark: find all transformed angles \(u=\frac{2\pi}{3},\pi,\frac{4\pi}{3}\).
  • 1 mark: apply \(x=\frac{u+\frac{\pi}{3}}{2}\) to every angle.
  • 1 mark: give the complete exact set \(\left\{\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{6}\right\}\).

starters.title: Preserve the zero-sine branch
starters.question: Solve \(\sin^2x=\sin x\cos x\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\).
starters.hint: Move everything to one side and use the zero-product rule.
starters.solution:
1. Factor \(\sin x(\sin x-\cos x)=0\).

  2. The first branch gives \(x=0,\pi,2\pi\). The second requires equal sine and cosine, giving \(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\).

  3. Combine both branches. Dividing by sine at the start would remove three valid angles.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{0,\ \frac{\pi}{4},\ \pi,\ \frac{5 \pi}{4},\ 2 \pi\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: rearrange and factor to \(\sin x(\sin x-\cos x)=0\).
  • 1 mark: keep the zero-sine branch \(x=0,\pi,2\pi\), including both endpoints.
  • 1 mark: solve the other branch \(\sin x=\cos x\) by a valid method.
  • 1 mark: obtain both additional angles \(x=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}\).
  • 1 mark: combine all five valid angles and list each once.

starters.title: A denominator removes one quadratic branch
starters.question: Solve \(\frac{2\sin^2x+\sin x-1}{\sin x+1}=0\) for \(-\pi\le x\le\pi\).
starters.hint: A zero numerator does not make an undefined fraction equal to zero.
starters.solution:
1. The original denominator requires \(\sin x\ne-1\), excluding \(x=-\frac{\pi}{2}\) in this interval.

  2. The numerator factors as \((2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)\). Only the branch \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\) remains allowed.

  3. The two allowed angles are \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\); both make the denominator nonzero.

  4. Therefore \(x\in \left\{\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5 \pi}{6}\right\}\) radians.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: state the original restriction \(\sin x\ne-1\).
  • 1 mark: factor the numerator as \((2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)\).
  • 1 mark: reject the forbidden branch \(\sin x=-1\) and retain \(\sin x=\frac{1}{2}\).

starters.title: Two quadratic-formula branches in a reversed interval
starters.question: Solve \(3\cos^2(60^\circ-2x)-\cos(60^\circ-2x)-1=0\) for \(0^\circ\le x\le180^\circ\). Give answers to one decimal place.
starters.hint: Both quadratic roots are possible. Each must be searched on the reversed transformed interval.
starters.solution:
1. Let \(u=60^\circ-2x\), giving \(-300^\circ\le u\le60^\circ\). Put \(t=\cos u\).

  2. The quadratic formula gives \(t=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}{6}\). Both values lie in \([-1,1]\).

  3. In degree mode, store \(\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}{6}\right)\) and \(\beta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{13}}{6}\right)\).

  4. The interval contains \(u=\alpha,-\alpha,-\beta,\beta-360^\circ\). Use \(x=\frac{60^\circ-u}{2}\) for each, then round.

  5. Therefore \(x\in \left\{10.1,\ 49.9,\ 87.9,\ 152.1\right\}\) degrees.

    Keep every valid angle and list a repeated angle only once.

  • 1 mark: use the quadratic formula on \(3t^2-t-1=0\), where \(t=\cos u\).
  • 1 mark: obtain \(t=\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}{6}\) and \(t=\frac{1-\sqrt{13}}{6}\), retaining both valid values.
  • 1 mark: find the two principal inverse-cosine values in degree mode and retain their full precision.
  • 1 mark: identify all four allowed transformed angles across the negative-to-positive interval.
  • 1 mark: apply \(x=\frac{60^\circ-u}{2}\) to all four angles.
  • 1 mark: give all four original angles to one decimal place, checking the original interval.

revision.body:
Solve the algebra, then find angles

Use a temporary variable, for example \(t=\sin x\). Factor or use

\[t=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}.\]

For sine and cosine, keep only \(-1\le t\le1\). Tangent can take any real ratio value. A repeated polynomial root is processed once, but it can still give several angles.

Choose an identity that leaves one ratio

\[\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x,\qquad\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x.\]

Match the squared replacement to the unsquared ratio. Keep brackets around the substituted expression. Remember that \(\sin^2x=(\sin x)^2\), not \(\sin(2x)\).

Preserve valid roots and exclusions

Bring terms to one side and factor. For a product equal to zero, solve each factor equation; do not divide away a possible zero factor.

For a fraction equal to zero, its numerator must be zero and its denominator nonzero. Record original exclusions before cancelling. After squaring, check every candidate in the original equation to restore the sign information.

Complete every branch on the interval

For a transformed argument \(u=bx+c\), transform both interval endpoints first. A negative multiplier reverses their order.

For every allowed ratio value, find all permitted values of \(u\), then use \(x=\frac{u-c}{b}\). Combine the angle sets, remove repeated entries and retain valid closed endpoints. Keep surds and inverse values unrounded until the final answer.
